stories.headline: Chart Reveals Democrats Dominating High-Income House Districts in 2026
stories.hook: A simple chart sorting U.S. House districts by income levels laid bare a striking shift: Democrats now lead in many wealthier areas after their midterm sweep.
stories.summary: Tom Wood's analysis showed Democratic-leaning districts clustering at the upper end of income rankings, marking a 'wild sorting' from recent cycles. Democrats secured 259 seats to Republicans' 173 in the November 2026 midterms, gaining ground in suburbs and higher-income zones. Observers like Robin Hanson called Democrats 'the party of the rich,' while others debated policies for middle-to-upper earners and ties to cultural divides.

stories.headline: Van Hollen Challenges Schumer for Senate Leadership Amid Israel Policy Clash
stories.hook: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen stepped up to challenge Chuck Schumer right after Democrats clinched a Senate majority, spotlighting deep party divides on Israel and lobbying pressures.
stories.summary: Van Hollen announced his bid for Senate leader shortly after the midterms, positioning himself as an underdog seeking bolder change against Schumer's long tenure. The race highlights sharp differences, with Van Hollen criticizing Israeli actions and AIPAC influence, while Schumer remains a firm U.S.-Israel ally. A closed-ballot vote among Senate Democrats is set for Dec. 1, and the outcome may reveal the party's stance on foreign policy and reform as the new Congress begins.

stories.headline: Conservatives Demand Thune Step Down Over SAVE Act Failure
stories.hook: Even after Republicans reelected Senate leader John Thune on November 10, conservative voices are rising with a clear message: pass the SAVE America Act or go.
stories.summary: Critics blame Thune for the Senate's failure to pass the SAVE America Act, which requires proof of citizenship to register and photo ID to vote, despite strong public support around 80-85% across parties and repeated House approvals. Republicans chose Thune by acclamation to lead as minority leader after midterm losses, but some pushed to delay the vote amid frustration. Sen. Mike Lee proposed debating the bill exhaustively to force a simple-majority vote, while defenders say it lacked the 60 votes needed to beat a filibuster. The tension highlights GOP divides on advancing election integrity measures.

stories.headline: Bush's 'No New Taxes' Pledge Draws Rejection from Republicans
stories.hook: George H.W. Bush's famous 1988 promise of 'Read my lips: No new taxes' resurfaced, but replies poured in dismissing any fondness for that era.
stories.summary: In 1988, Bush made the pledge at the Republican National Convention to set himself apart from Michael Dukakis, only to raise taxes two years later in a budget deal amid deficits, hurting his conservative support. Replies like Catturd's 'No, you're pretty much alone' and Derek Johnson's 'Naw… you’re not alone. There’s a few of you dumbasses' reject nostalgia, calling the pre-Trump GOP a 'fake, ineffective, surrender caucus' too quick to compromise. The thread highlights party divisions, with some favoring the old establishment style and others embracing Trump's populist America First shift as he serves as the 45th and 47th president.

stories.headline: Conservatives Slam Thune for Early Senate Adjournment
stories.hook: After the midterms flipped the Senate to Democrats, conservative voices erupted over Leader John Thune's decision to send senators home until November 30.
stories.summary: Users like Gunther Eagleman called Thune 'the problem with our GOP' and demanded his resignation, furious that the Thanksgiving recess wastes the lame-duck weeks of Republican control before January. They accuse him of blocking Trump priorities like the SAVE America Act for voter ID and citizenship proof, along with slowing nominees. Thune countered that the bill lacked votes against Democrats and accused influencers of stirring trouble, as the Senate eyes mid-December adjournment amid party tensions.

stories.headline: Debate Simmers Over Vance as Potential Successor to Trump
stories.hook: Photos of Trump and Vance side by side have users pondering a big what-if: who would lead better if Trump's term ended early?
stories.summary: A discussion weighs whether Vice President JD Vance would outperform Donald Trump as president in a hypothetical early succession from resignation or impeachment. Opinions split sharply, with some calling Vance more capable but riskier due to ties to billionaire Peter Thiel, labeled by critics as making him a 'lapdog' without principles, while others say he would be 'a better president than Trump could ever be.' The talk arises amid Republican midterm losses and Vance's plan to eye a 2028 run next year, reflecting uncertainty in party direction late 2026.

stories.headline: Senator-Elect Colom Prioritizes Mississippi Over Middle East Politics
stories.hook: Fresh off his upset win, Mississippi's Scott Colom admitted on radio that Middle East conflicts confuse him—and he'd rather tackle housing and jobs back home.
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom, the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, told The Clay Edwards Show on Nov. 24 that after two decades of U.S. wars abroad, he doesn't grasp Middle East politics and wants to focus on local needs like affordable homes, strong schools, and family-supporting jobs. His honest take drew praise for realism from some, while others argued senators must master foreign policy for votes on wars and aid. Colom clarified online that it's no dodge, but a call to recognize America's limits after years of involvement, aligning with his campaign against endless engagements.

stories.headline: Grassley Announces Trump Nominees Amid Conservative Backlash on Pace
stories.hook: Sen. Chuck Grassley shared plans for five Trump judicial nominees ready in December, but conservatives fired back, frustrated by what they see as two years of delays.
stories.summary: Grassley noted the Judiciary Committee will advance 13 more lifetime appointments out of committee despite a busy lame-duck schedule with funding and defense issues. Critics on the right blame the Senate's slow pace since Trump's election and target the 'blue slip' tradition that lets home-state senators stall district court picks. Defenders like attorney Mike Davis praised Grassley's work, while the committee has sped up recent votes to fill vacancies before Democrats take the majority in January. Grassley highlighted faster confirmations than recent decades, aiming for 300 Trump judges by year's end.
